newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dixie Hummingbirds wing their way to 70th year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dixie Hummingbirds wing their way to 70th year.

text.p: Their new CD won't top the charts and you shouldn't expect to see them on MTV, but after almost 70 years on the road the Dixie Hummingbirds are still going strong, serving up a potent brew of bluesy, soul-stirring gospel music.
Founded in South Carolina in 1928, but based in Philadelphia for over half a century, the Birds are led by their virtuoso lead singer Ira Tucker, 73, a group member for almost 60 years.
On a sunny summer evening in The Hague, Tucker and the other three Dixie Hummingbirds gave an open-air concert in a warm-up event for the city's annual jazz festival.

The subtle interplay of the four voices, backed only by the rhythmic chords and jazzy fills of guitarist Harold Carroll, slowly begins to work its spell on a small but increasingly appreciative crowd.
Most spectators had never heard of the group.
Carroll is another veteran member who joined in the early 1950s when gospel quartets started to add simple instrumental accompaniments to what had previously been a purely vocal music.
The current line-up is completed by Paul Owens, who rejoined in the late 1980s after an earlier defection to the Swan Silvertones, and Carl Davis who has also sung with the Swans.
Tucker, Owens and Davis share lead-singing duties, dropping back to sing harmony or set up syncopated call-and-response chants when theirs is not the featured voice.
The Birds' music spans a broad range of tempos and moods from slow and plaintive to upbeat, emotion-charged romps. Gradually, the crowd grew larger and their applause louder.
BIRDS DRAW PLAUDITS FROM FELLOW MUSICIANS
Gospel expert Anthony Heilbut heaped praise on the Dixie Hummingbirds in his book 'The Gospel Sound'.
"For versatility, imagination and harmony few groups play in their league." he enthused.
Ray Charles has acknowledged the powerful influence of gospel singers such as Tucker, Archie Brownlee of the Five Blind Boys of Mississippi and Claude Jeter of the Swan Silvertones.
"These guys have voices which could shake down your house and smash all the furniture in it. Jesus, could they wail!" Charles wrote in his autobiography 'Brother Ray'.
While the Dixie Hummingbirds and other pioneering black gospel artists have drawn plaudits from musicians and connoisseurs, broader public recognition has been limited.
Yet fans of soul singers like Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett and James Brown -- who all started as gospel singers -- would no doubt appreciate gospel's emotion and spontaneity.
From time to time the limelight has briefly shone on the Dixie Hummingbirds, such as in 1966 when they won a standing ovation at the Newport Folk Festival.
In 1973 they backed Paul Simon on his Top Ten hit "Loves Me Like a Rock" and went on to win a Grammy award for their own version of the song.
And two years ago the group's career was chronicled in a film of the same name made by Ashley James.
NEW COMPACT DISC PLANNED
Backstage after the show in The Hague, Ira Tucker patiently and politely answered questions from a reporter who turned up out of the blue without an appointment.
The Birds plan to record a new compact disc when they return to the United States, he said, and as usual he planned to write a fair share of the songs himself.
Although they have performed together so long, Tucker still believes practice makes perfect. Some 90 percent of what happens on stage is rehearsed and only 10 percent improvised, he says.
The same goes for arrangements of new songs. Sometimes they fall into place quite quickly, but if necessary the Birds will work on them for months to get them just right.
Tucker and the other members of the group are proud to keep the flame of traditional gospel music burning.
As he told Anthony Heilbut some years ago: "Gospel's the greatest music there is. Someday I'd just like to get that across to the people."
